p.src: Meanwhile, Granny Liu took Ban’er with her and first went to see Xifeng. “I must go home first thing tomorrow morning,” she said. “Though I have stayed only two or three days, I have experienced everything I had never before seen, tasted, or heard of in all my life. “It is rare indeed that the Old Lady, you, madam, all the young ladies, and even the maids in every apartment should have shown such compassion for my poverty and age and taken such good care of me. “When I return home, I shall have no other means of repaying you. I can only buy the finest incense and pray to the Buddha for you every day, asking that you all live to a hundred. That will be the token of my gratitude.” Xifeng laughed. “Do not be so pleased with yourself. “It is all because of you that the Old Lady caught a chill from the wind. She is lying down and says she feels unwell. Even my little girl has caught cold and is running a fever.” Hearing this, Granny Liu hastily sighed. “The Old Lady is advanced in years and is not accustomed to such exertion.” “She has never enjoyed herself as much as she did yesterday,” said Xifeng. “She often goes into the Garden for an outing, but ordinarily she merely sits awhile at one or two places before returning. “Yesterday, because you were here and she wanted to show you around, she walked through more than half the Garden. “As for my little girl, she came looking for me, and Her Ladyship gave her a piece of cake. Who could have known that eating it out in the wind would bring on a fever?” Granny Liu said, “I expect the little lady seldom enters the Garden. A strange place is somewhere a small child ought not to go in the first place. “She is not like our country children, who, once they can walk, will run through any graveyard they come upon. “For one thing, the wind may indeed have struck her; for another, because her person is pure and her eyes are clear, she may have encountered some spirit. “In my opinion, you should consult the book of malignant influences for her, in case some wandering spirit has afflicted her.” Her words reminded Xifeng, who told Ping’er to bring out The Jade Casket Record and have Caiming read from it. After turning the pages for a while, Caiming read aloud, “On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, the patient encountered the Flower Spirit in the southeast. “Take forty sheets of five-colored spirit money and convey the influence away at a point forty paces to the southeast. Great good fortune.” Xifeng laughed. “It is exactly right. Is not the Garden full of flower spirits? “I fear the Old Lady encountered one as well.” She at once ordered two portions of spirit money to be fetched and summoned two people: one to dispel the malignant influence from Grandmother Jia and the other to do the same for her little girl. Sure enough, the little girl soon slept peacefully.

p.src: Xifeng laughed. “After all, older people like you have much more experience. “My little girl is often falling ill, and I have never understood why.” Granny Liu replied, “Such things do happen. “Children raised in wealthy families are often too delicate and naturally cannot endure the slightest hardship. Besides, such a young child cannot bear being held in too much honor either. “It will be better if you dote on her a little less in the future, madam.” “There is sense in that,” said Xifeng. “Come to think of it, she still has no name. You must give her one. “For one thing, she may borrow some of your longevity. For another—and do not take offense—you country people live in poverty, so perhaps a name bestowed by a poor woman like you will be humble enough to keep her safe.” Hearing this, Granny Liu thought for a moment, then asked with a smile, “When was she born?” “The trouble is that the date of her birth was inauspicious,” said Xifeng. “As chance would have it, she was born on the seventh day of the seventh month.” Granny Liu promptly laughed. “Why, that is perfect! Let us call her Qiaoge’er. “This is the method of ‘fighting poison with poison and fire with fire.’ “If you will only accept the name I have chosen, madam, she is sure to live to a hundred. “When she grows up and everyone has established a household and livelihood of their own, should she ever meet with some disappointment, she will surely turn danger into good fortune and calamity into blessing—all through the power of this word qiao, ‘fortunate chance.’”

p.src: Granny Liu hurried after Ping'er into the room on the other side, where she saw gifts piled over half the kang. Ping'er showed them to her one by one, saying, “Here is the bolt of blue gauze you asked for yesterday, and Mistress has also given you a bolt of solid moon-white gauze for lining. These are two lengths of pongee, suitable for either jackets or skirts. Inside this bundle are two lengths of silk, so you can make yourself something to wear at New Year. This box contains assorted pastries made in the Imperial Household, some you have tasted and some you have not. Take them home and serve them on plates when you have guests; they are rather better than the ones you can buy. These are the two sacks in which you brought the melons and fruit yesterday. One now holds two dou of imperial-field polished rice, which makes exceptionally fine porridge; the other contains fruit from the garden and assorted dried fruits. This packet contains eight taels of silver. All these are from our mistress. These other two packets contain fifty taels each, making one hundred in all. They are from Her Ladyship, who says you are to use the money either to start some small business or to buy a few mu of land, so that henceforth you need no longer appeal to relatives and friends for help.” Then she added with a quiet smile, “These two jackets and two skirts, together with four headcloths and a packet of woollen thread, are my own gifts to you, Granny. The clothes are used, but I have scarcely worn them. If you think them beneath you, I shall be too ashamed to say another word.” At every item Ping'er named, Granny Liu invoked the Buddha, until by now she must have done so thousands of times. Seeing that Ping'er too was giving her so many things and was still so modest about it, she hastily invoked the Buddha again and said, “How can you say such a thing, miss? How could I possibly turn up my nose at such fine things! Even if I had the money, I would have nowhere to buy their like. I am only terribly embarrassed: it seems wrong to accept them, yet if I refuse, I shall be disappointing your kind intentions.” Ping'er smiled. “There is no need for such formality. I would not offer them if we were not all one family. Accept them without misgivings, for I shall be asking something of you in return. At the end of the year, just bring us some of the dried lamb's-quarters, cowpeas, hyacinth beans, eggplants, gourd strips, and the other dried vegetables you prepare. Everyone here, from the highest to the lowest, loves them. That will settle the matter. We want nothing else at all, so do not waste your thought and effort.” Granny Liu thanked her over and over and readily agreed. Ping'er said, “Go along now and get some sleep. I shall pack everything properly and leave it here. Early tomorrow morning I shall send the pages to hire a cart and load it all, so you need not trouble yourself in the least.”

p.src: Granny Liu's gratitude now knew no bounds. She returned to take leave of Xifeng with repeated thanks, then spent the night in Grandmother Jia's quarters. The next morning, as soon as she had washed and combed her hair, she prepared to say farewell. But Grandmother Jia was indisposed, so everyone came to inquire after her health, and a servant was sent to summon a physician. Before long, an old serving-woman reported that the physician had arrived. The senior maids urged Grandmother Jia to sit behind the bed-curtains. Grandmother Jia said, “I am an old woman now. What sort of creature could I not have borne and raised? Do you suppose I am afraid of him? Do not draw the curtains. Let him examine me as I am.” Hearing this, the serving-women brought over a small table, placed a little cushion on it, and ordered the physician to be shown in.

Do not draw the curtains. Let him examine me as I am.”
Hearing this, the serving-women brought over a small table, placed a little cushion on it, and ordered the physician to be shown in.

p.src: Presently Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, and Jia Rong appeared, escorting Imperial Physician Wang. Physician Wang did not dare use the central paved walk, but kept to the side steps and followed Jia Zhen up to the terrace. Two old serving-women were already holding up the curtains on either side, while two others led him in. Baoyu came out to meet him as well. Grandmother Jia sat upright on the couch, wearing a blue crinkled-silk jacket lined with pearl-fleece lambskin. On either side stood four little maids whose hair had not yet been put up, holding fly-whisks, rinsing bowls, and other articles. Five or six old nurses were ranged behind them like the wings of a wild goose, while beyond the green-gauze screen could be dimly seen a large company dressed in red and green and adorned with jewelled hairpins and pearls. Physician Wang dared not raise his eyes, but hurried forward to pay his respects. Seeing that he wore the insignia of the sixth rank, Grandmother Jia knew that he was an imperial physician and asked with a smile, “I trust you are well, Court Physician?” Then she asked Jia Zhen, “What is this Court Physician's honoured surname?” Jia Zhen and the others hastily replied, “Wang.” Grandmother Jia said, “In former days Wang Junxiao, the director of the Imperial Academy of Medicine, was excellent at taking the pulse.” Physician Wang at once bowed, lowered his head, and replied with a smile, “He was my great-uncle.” On hearing this, Grandmother Jia smiled. “So that is how it is. Then our families are old acquaintances.” As she spoke, she slowly extended her hand and laid it on the little cushion. An old nurse brought a low stool and quickly set it before the little table, slightly to one side. Physician Wang sat with one knee bent and, tilting his head, felt her pulse for a long while. He then examined the other wrist, rose slightly, bowed his head, and withdrew. Grandmother Jia said with a smile, “Thank you for your trouble. Zhen, see him out and have good tea served to him.”

p.src: Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, and the others repeatedly answered, “Yes,” then escorted Physician Wang back to the outer study. Physician Wang said, “The venerable lady has no other ailment; she has merely caught a slight chill. In truth, there is no need for medicine. If she eats somewhat lightly and keeps a little warmer, she will soon recover. I shall write a prescription and leave it here. If the old lady wishes to take it, prepare one dose according to the prescription; if she cannot be bothered, she may leave it alone.” With that, he drank his tea and wrote out the prescription. He was just about to take his leave when a nurse came out carrying little Dajie'er and said with a smile, “Would you examine our little girl too, Master Wang?” Hearing this, Physician Wang rose at once. While the child remained in the nurse's arms, he supported Dajie'er's hand with his left hand and felt her pulse with his right. Then he touched her forehead and asked her to put out her tongue so that he could inspect it. Smiling, he said, “I expect the young lady will scold me again, but all she needs is to fast quietly for a couple of meals, and she will be well. There is no need for a decoction. I shall send over some pills; at bedtime, dissolve them in ginger infusion and have her take them.” Having said this, he took his leave and departed.

p.src: Jia Zhen and the others took the prescription back, explained the circumstances to Grandmother Jia, placed it on the table, and withdrew. Nothing further need be said of them. Meanwhile, Lady Wang, Li Wan, Xifeng, Baochai and the other girls waited until the physician had left before emerging from behind the screen. Lady Wang sat for a short while, then returned to her own rooms.

p.src: When Granny Liu saw that nothing more was required, she came forward to take her leave of Grandmother Jia. Grandmother Jia said, “Come again when you have time.” Then she summoned Yuanyang and said, “See that Granny Liu is properly attended to on her way out. I am not feeling well and cannot see you off myself.” Granny Liu thanked her and took her leave once more, then went out with Yuanyang. When they reached the servants’ quarters, Yuanyang pointed to a bundle on the kang and said, “These are several garments belonging to the Old Lady. They were presented to her by various people on birthdays and festivals in past years. She never wears clothes made by others, and it would be a pity merely to store them away, though not one has ever been worn. Yesterday she told me to take out two outfits for you to carry home. Give them away or let your own family wear them, as you please—and do not laugh at such a gift. This box contains the flour pastries you asked for. This parcel contains the medicines you mentioned the other day: Plum-Blossom Tongue-Spotting Pills, Purple-Gold Tablets, Tendon-Quickening Pills, and Life-Preserving Childbirth Pills. Each kind is wrapped with its prescription, and they are all bundled together inside. And here are two purses for you to keep as playthings.” As she spoke, she loosened the cords, took out two small silver ingots fashioned with the rebus ‘brush, tablet, and ruyi,’ and showed them to her. Then she laughed and said, “Take the purses, but leave these with me.” Granny Liu was already beside herself with joy and had invoked the Buddha thousands of times over. Hearing Yuanyang say this, she replied, “By all means keep them, miss.” Seeing that she had taken the joke seriously, Yuanyang put them back into the purses and laughed. “I was only teasing you. I have plenty of them. Keep them to give to the children at New Year.” Just then a little maid came in carrying a Cheng-ware cup, which she handed to Granny Liu. “This is for you from Second Master Bao.” Granny Liu exclaimed, “Whatever can I say to this? What merit can I have earned in some former life to be treated like this today?” With that, she accepted it. Yuanyang said, “The clothes you changed into when I had you bathe the other day are mine. If you do not disdain them, I have several more and will give those to you as well.” Granny Liu hurriedly thanked her again. Sure enough, Yuanyang brought out two more garments and wrapped them up for her. Granny Liu then wished to go into the Garden to thank Baoyu, the young ladies, Lady Wang, and the others before leaving. “There is no need to go,” said Yuanyang. They are not receiving visitors just now. I shall convey your farewells when I return. Come again when you have time.” She then summoned an old serving woman and instructed her, “Go to the second gate and call two pages to carry Granny’s things and escort her out.” The woman assented and accompanied Granny Liu to Xifeng’s quarters to collect the rest of her things. At the side gate she had the pages carry everything outside, and they escorted Granny Liu all the way to her cart. There is no need to dwell upon it.

p.src: Now Baocai and the others, after breakfast and a visit to Grandmother Jia to pay their respects, returned to the Garden. When they reached the fork in the paths, Baocai called to Daiyu, “Pin’er, come with me. I have something to ask you.” Daiyu accompanied Baocai to Allspice Court. Once inside, Baocai seated herself and said with a smile, “Kneel down. I am going to interrogate you.” Daiyu, unable to imagine why, laughed and said, “Just look—the Bao girl has gone mad! What are you going to interrogate me about?” Baocai gave a cold laugh. “What a fine young lady of rank you are! What a fine sheltered maiden who never leaves her chamber! And what was all that you were saying? You had better tell me the truth.” Still not understanding, Daiyu kept laughing, though inwardly she could not help growing suspicious. All she said was, “When did I ever say anything? You are merely trying to catch me out in some mistake. Tell me what it is, and let me hear it.” Baocai smiled. “You are still pretending innocence. What did you say during yesterday’s drinking game? I cannot imagine where those words came from.” Daiyu thought for a moment and at last remembered that, through carelessness the day before, she had quoted two lines from The Peony Pavilion and The Romance of the Western Chamber. Her face reddened at once. She came forward, put her arms around Baocai, and said with a smile, “Dear sister, I truly did not know; the words just slipped out. Teach me better, and I shall never say such things again.” Baocai laughed. “I do not know either. What you said sounded so unfamiliar that I wanted you to enlighten me.” “Dear sister,” said Daiyu, “please do not tell anyone else. I shall never say such things again.” Seeing her face flushed crimson with shame and hearing her plead so earnestly, Baocai would not press her further. She drew Daiyu down to sit and drink tea, then gently confided, “Who do you suppose I am? I too was once a mischievous child. When I was seven or eight, I was troublesome enough to wear anyone out. Our family may be counted among scholarly households, and in my grandfather’s day he was fond of collecting books. In those days our household was large, and all the sisters and brothers lived together, but none of us cared to read respectable books. Some of the boys were fond of poetry and some of lyric verse, and we had every sort of book—the Western Chamber, The Lute, and the Hundred Plays of the Yuan, among others. They would read them secretly behind our backs, while we in turn read them secretly behind theirs. Later, when the elders found out, some of us were beaten, some scolded, and the books were burned; only then did we give them up. That is why it is actually better for girls like us not to know how to read. Even men who read without learning sound principles are worse than men who never read at all—how much more must that be true of you and me? Even composing poetry and practicing calligraphy are not truly duties belonging to you and me; indeed, they are not ultimately the proper duties of men either. It is enough if men read to understand sound principles, assist the state, and govern the people. Yet nowadays one never hears of anyone like that. On the contrary, men become worse after reading books.

p.src: The books have led them astray, while they, regrettably, have also brought books into disrepute. They would actually do less harm if they farmed or traded instead. You and I ought simply to devote ourselves to needlework, sewing, spinning, and weaving. Since, unfortunately, we have learned to read, we should confine ourselves to respectable books. The greatest danger is that miscellaneous books may alter our temperaments; once that happens, there can be no saving us.” Throughout this speech Daiyu sat with lowered head, sipping her tea. Inwardly convinced, she could only answer with the single word, “Yes.” Suddenly Suyun came in and said, “Our mistress asks both young ladies to come and discuss an important matter. The Second, Third, and Fourth Young Ladies, Miss Shi, and Second Master Bao are all waiting there.” “What is it this time?” asked Baocai. Daiyu said, “We shall know when we get there.” With that, she and Baocai went to Paddy-Sweet Cottage, where, sure enough, they found everyone assembled.

p.src: When Li Wan saw the two of them, she laughed and said, “The society has not even begun, yet already someone is shirking her duties. Fourth Sister wants a whole year’s leave.” Daiyu laughed. “It is all because of something Grandmother said yesterday. She told her to paint some sort of picture of the garden, and that delighted her so much she asked for leave.” Tanchun laughed. “You must not blame Grandmother either. It all began with something Grannie Liu said.” Lin Daiyu hastily laughed and said, “That is true—it was all because of something she said. What sort of ‘grannie’ is she, anyway? We may as well call her a ‘mother locust.’” At this, everyone burst out laughing. Baochai laughed. “Any joke in the world reaches perfection once it passes through Sister Feng’s lips. Fortunately, Sister Feng is illiterate and not very learned, so her jokes are merely vulgar banter. But then there is sharp-tongued Pin’er: she applies the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals to such coarse popular sayings, extracting their essence, cutting away the excess, and polishing them with a telling comparison, until every sentence hits its mark. Those three words, ‘mother locust,’ conjure up the whole scene from yesterday. And how quick she was to think of it!” When the others heard this, they all laughed. “That commentary of yours is every bit as good as the jokes of those two.” Li Wan said, “I asked you all here to decide how many days’ leave we should give her. I offered her one month, but she thought it too little. What do you say?” Daiyu said, “Strictly speaking, even a year would not be too much. It took a whole year just to build this garden, so naturally it will take two years to paint it. She must grind the ink, dip the brush, spread the paper, apply the colors, and then…” She had only reached this point when everyone realized she was teasing Xichun, and they laughingly asked, “And then what else?” Daiyu herself could no longer suppress her laughter. “And then she must paint as slowly as she is doing now—how could that take less than two years?” Everyone clapped their hands and laughed without end. Baochai laughed. “‘And then she must paint as slowly as she is doing now’—that final line is the cleverest of all. That is why, amusing as yesterday’s jokes were, they seem rather tasteless when recalled. But think carefully about Pin’er’s few mild words: the more one recalls them, the more flavor they have. I have laughed so hard I cannot move.” Xichun said, “It is all because Sister Bao keeps praising her and making her bolder. Now she has begun making fun of me too.” Daiyu quickly took her hand and laughed. “Let me ask you first: are you to paint only the garden, or are you to put all of us into the picture too?” Xichun said, “At first I was told to paint only the garden, but yesterday Grandmother said that a picture of the garden alone would look like an architectural plan. She told me to include the people as well, so that it would resemble a pleasure-scene painting.

p.src: But I cannot paint such finely detailed towers and pavilions, nor can I paint people; yet I cannot very well refuse. That is precisely what is troubling me.” Daiyu said, “People are easy enough. It is insects that you cannot manage.” Li Wan said, “Now you are talking nonsense again. What possible need would there be for insects in such a picture? A bird or two might perhaps be added as decoration.” Daiyu laughed. “Never mind the other insects, but if yesterday’s ‘mother locust’ is left out, would that not spoil the allusion?” At this, everyone burst out laughing again. Clutching her chest with both hands as she laughed, Daiyu said, “Hurry and paint it. I have even composed the inscription for you. We shall call it The Grand Repast with a Locust in Tow.” Hearing this, everyone roared even louder, rocking back and forth with laughter. Suddenly there came a heavy thump. Not knowing what had fallen, they hurriedly looked around and saw that it was Xiangyun. She had been leaning over the back of a chair, which had not been standing firmly in the first place. With her whole weight pressed against it as she laughed, and being entirely off guard, she and the chair pulled in opposite directions; it tilted eastward, and both chair and girl toppled sideways. Fortunately, the wooden partition stopped them, and they did not fall to the floor. At the sight, everyone laughed harder than ever. Baoyu hurried over and helped her up, and only then did their laughter gradually subside. Baoyu gave Daiyu a meaningful glance. Understanding him, Daiyu went into the inner room, uncovered the mirror, and looked at herself. Seeing that the hair at her temples had loosened slightly, she quickly opened Li Wan’s dressing case, took out a small smoothing brush, and passed it twice over her hair before the mirror. Once she had put herself in order again, she came out, pointed at Li Wan, and said, “You were supposed to lead us in needlework and teach us proper conduct, yet instead you have gathered us here for wild sport and laughter.” Li Wan laughed. “Just listen to her artful tongue! She was the one who led the mischief and set everyone laughing, yet now she blames me for it. I am so vexed that I can only pray you will someday get a formidable mother-in-law, along with several fiendishly spiteful elder and younger sisters-in-law. Then we shall see whether you can still be so sharp-tongued!”

p.src: Lin Daiyu had already flushed crimson. Taking Baochai by the hand, she said, “Let us give her a year’s leave.” Baochai said, “I have a fair word to say; hear me out. Though Lotus can paint, she has done little more than a few freehand sketches. To paint this garden, one must have several landscapes already composed in one’s mind before a true picture can emerge. The garden itself is like a painting: its rocks and trees, towers and houses, their distances and spacing, are neither too much nor too little, but exactly as they should be. But if you simply copy it just as it stands onto paper, the result will certainly not be pleasing. You must consider the dimensions and perspective of the paper, decide where there should be more or less, distinguish principal elements from subordinate ones, add what should be added, remove what should be removed, conceal what should be concealed, and reveal what should be revealed. Only after making a draft and then studying and revising it carefully will you have a proper design. Secondly, all these towers and buildings must be drawn with ruler-guided architectural lines. At the slightest lapse of attention, the railings will lean, the pillars collapse, the doors and windows stand upside down, the steps split apart—even the tables may be squeezed into the walls and flowerpots set upon the curtains. Would that not turn the picture into a veritable joke? Thirdly, when figures are added, their grouping must also vary in density and height. The folds of robes, the ribbons of skirts, fingers, feet, and gait are most important. If a single stroke lacks precision, a hand will look swollen or a leg twisted; botching a face or hair is a lesser matter by comparison. In my view, the task is exceedingly difficult. A year’s leave is too much, while a month is too little. Let us give her half a year and assign Brother Bao to assist her. It is not that Brother Bao knows enough to teach her painting—that would only make matters worse. But whenever something is unclear or difficult to place, he can take it outside and consult the gentlemen who know how to paint; that will make things easier.”

p.src: Delighted at this, Baoyu immediately said, “That is perfectly right. Zhan Ziliang is superb at finely detailed towers and pavilions, and Cheng Rixing’s beauties are masterly. I shall go ask them at once.” Baochai said, “When I call you a meddlesome busybody, this is what I mean: no sooner is something mentioned than you rush off to ask. Wait until everything has been settled before you go. For now, what is she to paint on?” Baoyu replied, “We have Snow-Wave paper at home. It is large and takes ink well.” Baochai sneered, “I knew you would be no use! Snow-Wave paper is suitable for calligraphy, freehand painting, or Southern School landscapes by someone skilled in landscape painting. It takes ink well and withstands repeated texture strokes. If used for this picture, it will neither hold the colors nor take washes easily; the painting will be poor and the paper wasted. I will show you a way. When this garden was first built, there was a detailed plan. Though drawn by craftsmen, its scale and orientation are accurate. Ask Her Ladyship for it, then obtain from Sister Feng a piece of heavy silk matching the paper’s dimensions. Have one of the gentlemen size it with alum, and ask him to use the plan as a basis, making the necessary omissions and additions to establish the draft. Then all that remains is to add the figures. They will also have to prepare the mineral blues and greens, as well as the powdered gold and silver. You must also set up separate braziers for melting and refining glue and washing brushes. You will also need a large oil-finished table covered with felt. Your dishes and brushes are both incomplete; it would be best to procure an entirely new set.” Xichun said, “When have I ever possessed all those painting implements? I merely paint with whatever writing brushes happen to be at hand. As for pigments, I have only ocher, Canton blue, gamboge, and rouge. Besides those, I have nothing but two coloring brushes, and that is all.” Baochai said, “You should have said so earlier. I do have some of these things, but you had no use for them, so giving them to you would only have left them lying idle. For now I shall keep them for you. When you need such things, I will give you some, though they are fit only to save for painting fans; it would be a pity to use them on so large a picture. Today I shall make a list for you; take it to the Old Lady and ask her for the things on it. None of you is likely to know the whole list. I shall dictate, and Brother Bao can write it down.” Baoyu had already prepared brush and inkstone, for he had feared that he might not remember everything clearly and intended to write it down. Hearing Baochai say this, he joyfully raised his brush and listened attentively.

p.src: Baochai began: “Four number-one flat brushes, four number-two flat brushes, four number-three flat brushes; four large wash brushes, four medium wash brushes, four small wash brushes; ten large southern crab-claw brushes, ten small crab-claw brushes, ten beard-and-brow brushes; twenty large coloring brushes, twenty small coloring brushes, ten face-detail brushes, and twenty willow-twig brushes; four liang of Arrowhead Vermilion, four liang of Southern Ocher, four liang each of mineral yellow, mineral blue, and mineral green, four liang of tube yellow, eight liang of Canton blue, four boxes of shell white, ten cakes of rouge, two hundred sheets of large red flying gold, two hundred sheets of blue gold, four liang of fine Canton glue, and four liang of purified alum. The glue and alum used to size the silk are separate; do not concern yourself with them. Simply send the silk out and have them size it. We shall wash, settle, levigate, and refine these pigments ourselves. We can amuse ourselves with them as well as use them, and I assure you there will be enough to last your whole life. In addition, four sieves of the finest silk, four coarse silk sieves, four carrying brushes, four mortars of assorted sizes, twenty large coarse bowls, ten five-inch coarse dishes, twenty three-inch coarse white dishes, two braziers, four earthenware pots of assorted sizes, two new porcelain jars, four new water buckets, four one-foot white-cloth bags, twenty jin of light charcoal, one jin of willow charcoal, one three-drawer wooden chest, one zhang of close-woven gauze, two liang of fresh ginger, and half a jin of bean paste.” Daiyu hastily added, “One iron wok and one spatula.” Baochai asked, “What would those be for?” Daiyu laughed. “Since you want seasonings like ginger and bean paste, I thought I would ask for an iron wok as well, so you can stir-fry the pigments and eat them.” Everyone burst out laughing. Baochai laughed and said, “What do you know about it? Those coarse pigment dishes may well have to be heated over a fire. Unless their bottoms are first coated with ginger juice and bean paste and then baked, they will crack as soon as they are put over the flame.” When the others heard this, they all said, “So that is why.”

The glue and alum used to size the silk are separate; do not concern yourself with them. Simply send the silk out and have them size it.
We shall wash, settle, levigate, and refine these pigments ourselves. We can amuse ourselves with them as well as use them, and I assure you there will be enough to last your whole life.

In addition, four sieves of the finest silk, four coarse silk sieves, four carrying brushes, four mortars of assorted sizes, twenty large coarse bowls, ten five-inch coarse dishes, twenty three-inch coarse white dishes, two braziers, four earthenware pots of assorted sizes, two new porcelain jars, four new water buckets, four one-foot white-cloth bags, twenty jin of light charcoal, one jin of willow charcoal, one three-drawer wooden chest, one zhang of close-woven gauze, two liang of fresh ginger, and half a jin of bean paste.”
Daiyu hastily added, “One iron wok and one spatula.”
Baochai asked, “What would those be for?”
Daiyu laughed. “Since you want seasonings like ginger and bean paste, I thought I would ask for an iron wok as well, so you can stir-fry the pigments and eat them.”
Everyone burst out laughing.
Baochai laughed and said, “What do you know about it?

Those coarse pigment dishes may well have to be heated over a fire. Unless their bottoms are first coated with ginger juice and bean paste and then baked, they will crack as soon as they are put over the flame.”
When the others heard this, they all said, “So that is why.”

p.src: Daiyu studied the list for a while longer, then laughingly drew Tanchun aside and whispered, “Just look! All these water jars and chests are wanted merely to paint a picture. She must have grown muddleheaded and added her dowry list as well.” Tanchun gave an exclamation and could not stop laughing. “Cousin Bao,” she said, “aren’t you going to twist her mouth? Ask her why she is making such remarks about you.” “Why ask?” Baochai replied with a smile. “Can ivory ever come from a dog’s mouth?” As she spoke, she came over, pushed Daiyu down upon the kang, and made as if to pinch her face. Laughing, Daiyu hastily pleaded, “Dear sister, spare me! Little Pin is young and knows only how to talk, without knowing what may or may not be said; as my elder sister, you must teach me better. If you will not forgive me, whom else can I turn to?” The others, unaware of the meaning behind her words, all laughed and said, “She sounds so pitiful that even our hearts have softened. Do spare her.” Baochai had only meant to tease her, but when she heard Daiyu allude again to the earlier occasion on which she had reproved her for indiscriminately reading improper books, she felt it would be awkward to continue romping with her and let her up. Daiyu laughed. “You truly are a good elder sister. If it were I, I would never let anyone off.” Pointing at her with a smile, Baochai said, “No wonder the Old Lady dotes on you and everyone loves you for your cleverness. Today even I have grown exceedingly fond of you. Come here, and let me smooth your hair for you.” Daiyu obediently turned around, and Baochai reached out to smooth her hair. Watching from beside them, Baoyu thought she looked lovelier still. He could not help regretting that he had told her to smooth back the hair at her temples; he should have left it loose so that he could now ask Baochai to dress it for her. While he was indulging in these idle thoughts, Baochai said, “Now that the list is finished, report to the Old Lady tomorrow. Whatever the household already has need not be bought; as for anything it lacks, take some money and purchase it, and I shall help you assemble everything.” Baoyu hurriedly put the list away.

p.src: They chatted idly for a while longer. After the evening meal, they went once more to pay their respects to Grandmother Jia. Grandmother Jia had never been seriously ill; she had merely tired herself and caught a slight chill. After resting comfortably for a day and taking a dose of medicine to dispel it, she was well again by evening. What was said and done the following day remains to be told in the next chapter.
